A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UPD/JUPD research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Overcooked-AI and OGC experiments, ablations, partner-curriculum analyses, and a 12-participant human-AI study.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on LBF, Overcooked-AI, and OGC, including revised baseline results, additional analyses, and human-AI study outcomes.

M1.justification: The ego/random policy mixture, Dirichlet bias, variance-based selection, PPO architecture, and joint partner-level approach remain. The stated JUPD scoring rule gains a numerical stabilizer: v1 divides by squared mean return, whereas v2 uses (mean + delta)^2, with delta = 10^-8 (v1 Equation 5; v2 Equation 6 and Table 7).

E1.justification: v2 adds Level-Based Foraging: two-agent cooperative food collection on a 7x7 grid with ten evaluation partners, extending coverage beyond the retained Overcooked-AI and OGC tasks. The reported human age range also changes from 26–34 to 22–31; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects different recruitment or a correction.

E2.justification: v2 adds ROTATE as an evaluated Overcooked comparator in Appendix D, Table 3, and the per-partner comparison in Figure 20. v1 already cited ROTATE but did not evaluate it. The original SP, FCP, MEP, E3T, human-study, and OGC comparator memberships are retained.

E3.justification: Reported Overcooked settings change materially: FCP/MEP best-response training moves from up to 100 million steps to 50 million, and UPD's generated-partner batch changes from 8,192 to 4,000. v2 also revises SP and layout-specific MEP configurations and introduces LBF epsilon sweeps, ROTATE-specific budgets and architecture, and layout-tuned UPD protocols. Appendix B explicitly confirms rerunning affected baseline experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of E3T's epsilon sensitivity in LBF, benefits from layout-specific UPD curriculum tuning, and curriculum dynamics for UPD without bias or learnability filtering (Appendices D and J.1.2; Figure 21). These examine tuning sensitivity and the mechanism behind convention changes. The original alternative-score comparison and checkpoint-based learnability/return analyses are retained, partly relocated.

E5.justification: v2 introduces explicit three-seed replication for the new ROTATE and fine-tuned UPD comparisons, including ROTATE seed identifiers. Existing main comparisons retain six seeds and mean ± standard deviation reporting. Human-study Wilcoxon tests, paired t-tests, Holm correction, and reliability estimation remain; changed statistical values alone are results changes.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerous estimates: FCP's average changes from 45.2 ± 11.2 to 70.0 ± 2.2, while UPD remains 94.4 but its reported deviation changes from 8.1 to 2.3; UPD also loses its CRoom lead. These revised configurations and corrected experiments do not establish same-setting gains. v2 adds LBF, ROTATE, and tuned-UPD results, revises alternative-score and human-rating results, and changes Cronbach's alpha from 0.938 to 0.916. OGC mean returns remain, but aggregate deviations change.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the general Dec-UPOMDP presentation with a two-agent stochastic-game formalism and explicitly derives partner-conditioned transitions and rewards. It adds a policy-improvement argument invoking Foster et al., a coordination-game analysis (Section 4.4 and Appendix C), and computational-cost derivations (Appendix F). It also corrects adaptive success-rate p from a binary indicator to the fraction of rollouts exceeding the global median, avoiding the identically zero p(1-p) implied by v1's written definition.

C1.justification: The population-free adaptive partner curriculum and joint partner-environment contributions remain central. However, v2 drops the explicit first-method claim and narrows the abstract/introduction/conclusion's consistent-outperformance and significant human-return-superiority commitments to strong comparative performance. This limits novelty and performance claims without replacing the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 attributes much of the improvement to partner generation and biasing, with learnability supplying an additional gain, and adds interpretations linking convention changes to generation plus selection. It introduces human-sample-size qualifications and dependence of computational advantages on inexpensive, vectorized simulation. v1's explicit discussion of discrete-action/behavioral-diversity limits and artificial-versus-human ranking discrepancies is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation provenance, population construction and checkpoint selection, baseline-specific settings, JUPD sampling and buffer details, and ROTATE/tuned-UPD parameter tables. It newly documents the sampling ratio, stability constant, 200-step human games, and experimenter blinding. Its transparency note discloses earlier baseline implementation/configuration problems. These disclosures go well beyond v1's more general reproducibility information.

R1.justification: v2 broadens citations and discussion to classic model-based AHT, offline/generative partner models, and Foster et al.'s learnability argument, while retaining the central E3T/SFL positioning. Eysenbach et al. and Oliehoek–Amato references disappear. ROTATE was already cited in v1, and publication updates to retained works do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, method exposition, discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. The four-question experimental narrative becomes separate fixed-environment and procedural-generation sections. Method subsections are reordered, alternative-learnability material moves into the appendix, and the appendices are substantially reorganized. This exceeds changes required merely to insert new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds LBF and ablation-dynamics plots, ROTATE/tuning results and parameter tables, and percentage-comparison columns. It redisplays existing appendix scatterplots in the main text, relocates the alternative-score plot, expands the per-partner chart, and redraws the kitchen layouts. The conference template and predominantly single-column appendix also substantially change visual organization.

improvement.justification: Correcting and rerunning faulty baseline experiments addresses an important weakness in v1's comparative evidence. The ROTATE and LBF evaluations, fuller reproducibility information, and narrower performance claims substantially strengthen the paper. Limitations remain: human-study episode accounting is inconsistent, and the new uniform-partner toy example does not itself establish expected policy improvement because every ego policy receives expected reward 0.5. These issues temper the theoretical gains, but the improved empirical comparisons and transparency provide a substantial net benefit.
